props.title: A separate CI server vs. Actions

items: A server you host, patch and back up
Lives inside GitHub, next to your code
Built in — nothing to wire up
Reacts to dozens of GitHub events

captions: Part one. The big picture.

Before any YAML, let's understand the problem
Actions solves.
Two ideas sit underneath everything.

First, continuous integration, or CI. Everyone
merges small changes

often, and every merge is automatically built and
tested.
Problems surface in minutes, not weeks.

Second, continuous delivery, or CD. Once a change
passes,

it's automatically packaged and shipped — to
staging, then
to production.

Together they form a loop. Code, build, test,
release,
deploy, monitor — and back to code.
The faster that loop spins, the faster a team
learns. GitHub Actions is the engine that spins it.
There are other tools for this — Jenkins, CircleCI,
GitLab CI. So why Actions?
The big difference is where it lives. Actions runs
inside GitHub, right next to your code, your pull
requests and your issues.
No separate server to patch. No webhooks to wire
up.
And it's not just for CI. Actions reacts to
almost any event on GitHub — a new issue,
a comment, a release, a schedule.

So it's really a general automation platform that
happens
to be great at CI/CD.

Now the mental model. Five words, and everything
else
hangs off them.
An event is something that happens — like a
push.
The event triggers a workflow: a YAML file in
your repository.
A workflow contains one or more jobs.
Each job runs on a runner — a fresh
virtual machine.
And each job is a list of steps, run
in order. A step either runs a shell command,
or uses a prebuilt action.
Event, workflow, job, runner, step. Hold on to that
chain. Every chapter from here zooms into one link
of it.
